strengths: Timely and well-motivated contribution: the paper targets a genuine gap in evaluating long-form text-to-video generation under complex prompts, and Table 1 convincingly situates LoCoT2V-Bench against prior benchmarks (longest, most complex prompt suite).

The prompt suite construction is thoughtful: 240 prompts across 18 themes derived from real-world YouTube videos, with self-refine based MLLM generation plus manual review, and explicit incorporation of scene transitions, camera motion, and event dynamics.

The multi-dimensional evaluation framework contains genuinely novel components beyond prior work, e.g., event-level alignment with Hungarian matching and inversion-based temporal order penalty (Eq. 1), transition smoothness, and intra-/inter-event subject/background consistency grounded in event boundaries.

Empirical analysis goes beyond a leaderboard: the authors probe metric entanglement (Sec 4.4), correlation between static quality and other dimensions (Sec 4.3), and prompt-complexity effects (Sec 4.5), which strengthens the credibility of the benchmark.

Broad baseline coverage: nine representative LVG methods spanning training-free extension, autoregressive, and agent-based pipelines, with implementation details in the appendix; findings (weak inter-event coherence, fine-grained alignment, narrative adherence) are concrete and actionable.
Mathematical descriptions of the consistency metrics and full prompt templates in appendices B.7-C.6 support transparency of the evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: Critical soundness gap: the benchmark relies almost entirely on MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Seed1.5-VL, DeepSeek-V3.1) as evaluators, yet no human study is reported to validate that these automated metrics (especially HERD, content clarity, and overall/event-level alignment) correlate with human judgment. 'HERD' implies human expectations but involves no human raters; this is a major omission for a benchmark paper whose central contribution is the metrics themselves.

Potential circularity and evaluator bias: prompts are generated from videos by VLMs, alignment is scored by comparing a VLM-generated video description to the prompt base, and HERD questions are generated by VLMs from VLM assessments. The choice of Qwen2.5-VL-7B (a relatively small model for long-video understanding) and sensitivity of results to the evaluator model are not analyzed; results could be substantially artifacts of evaluator limitations rather than generation-model weaknesses.

Several metric formulations appear ad-hoc and under-validated: Eq. 4 introduces scaling factor b and constant c without values or sensitivity analysis; the RR-UB normalization for aesthetic quality is heuristic; Eq. 1's product-of-similarities design is not compared against alternatives.

Reproducibility is currently weak: code is not released ('full release will be made after code reorganization'), and results depend on many interacting third-party tools and models (Time-R1, Grounded-SAM-2, PySceneDetect, RAFT, DOVER++), making faithful reimplementation difficult at submission time.

Only open-source methods are evaluated despite citing Sora, Veo, and Kling; some baselines (FreeNoise, FreeLong, FIFO-Diffusion) are relatively dated, so conclusions about 'current methods' may be driven by an unrepresentative baseline set.

Statistical rigor is limited: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance analysis over the 240 samples for most headline results; some differences in Tables 2-4 appear small relative to likely measurement noise.

Presentation issues reduce polish: a typo ('adpot'), grammar problems, section C.5 is titled 'Content Clarity Evaluation Prompt' but contains the HERD prompt, the reproducibility statement contains a dangling sentence, and Appendix B.6/B.7 are referenced inconsistently (transition smoothness details cited as B.6 in main text but the label ordering differs).

Floor effects concern: event-level alignment scores range roughly 23-60% and HERD narrative flow ~19-35%, suggesting the benchmark may saturate near the bottom of the scale for current models, limiting its discriminative power for ranking similar methods; this is acknowledged implicitly but not analyzed.

strengths: Addresses a timely and genuinely under-served problem: systematic evaluation of long-form text-to-video generation under complex, realistic prompts, where existing benchmarks (VBench-Long, VBench-2.0) rely on short or simplified prompts (Table 1 comparison is a reasonable positioning argument).

The prompt construction pipeline (real YouTube videos across 18 themes -> MLLM generation with self-refine -> manual factual review -> integration of per-dimension evaluation metadata) yields prompts with substantially higher length/complexity than prior suites, and the statistics and word clouds are transparently reported.

The multi-dimensional framework is broad and thoughtfully organized: five dimensions with 26 sub-metrics, several of which are non-trivial and novel for long video evaluation (event-level alignment with Hungarian matching and inversion penalty, intra-/inter-event temporal consistency via event segmentation, transition smoothness, and the polarity-aware binary-question HERD scheme).

Beyond a leaderboard, the paper includes useful meta-analyses: correlation of static quality with other dimensions (bias check), entanglement between event-level alignment and temporal consistency, and the effect of prompt complexity on outcomes; these analyses are a model of due diligence for benchmark design.
Nine open-source LVG methods are evaluated under a unified protocol with implementation details in the appendix, and prompts are released in JSON, partially supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: No human validation of the metrics. For a benchmark whose flagship metric is 'Human Expectation Realization Degree', there is zero human study: no correlation of any dimension with human judgments, no human preference ranking of the nine models to compare against the metric rankings. All 'high-level' judgments (content clarity, HERD) are made by MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, DeepSeek-V3.1, Seed1.5-VL), so the benchmark effectively measures MLLM expectation, not human expectation. This is a fundamental evidential gap for the central claim.

Circularity and potential self-consistency bias: prompts are generated from videos by MLLMs, event extraction is by DeepSeek-V3.1, alignment is scored by embedding similarity between a Qwen2.5-VL-7B caption and a prompt produced from that same generation pipeline, and HERD questions are generated from MLLM assessments of the source videos and then answered by an MLLM. No ablation over judge models is provided, so the community cannot assess how sensitive scores are to the choice of judge, nor whether the pipeline's shared LLM biases inflate apparent alignment.

Key design decisions are under-justified: the 'prompt base' (rather than the raw prompt) is used for alignment scoring; the product of semantic and average field similarities in Eq. (1) is arbitrary; the inversion penalty scaling and the abruptness normalization (Eq. 4 with unspecified b, c, alpha weights) are not analyzed for sensitivity; the RR-UB normalization for aesthetic quality depends on a top-10% cut over one generated-image subset without justification.

The entanglement analysis in Section 4.4 is essentially a post-hoc rationalization of a design flaw: the paper admits that temporal-consistency scores can be high for videos that never realize the described events, yet these metrics are still aggregated into the temporal-quality dimension that feeds the headline table and rankings.

No statistical treatment: single runs, no confidence intervals, no seed variance, and 240 prompts may be too few to support fine-grained conclusions (e.g., the 'minor differences across theme categories' claim in 4.2).

Fairness of the comparison is questionable: multi-prompt methods receive LLM-generated event-level prompts while others receive the full prompt; models differ in supported duration/resolution (e.g., SkyReels-V2 540P), and the paper does not discuss how output length mismatch affects metrics like transition smoothness or event count.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the evaluation code and full results are promised only 'after code reorganization', so the many custom tool pipelines (Time-R1, Grounded-SAM-2, PySceneDetect, RAFT, DOVER++, judge LLMs) cannot currently be re-run or verified.

Presentation issues undermine polish: 'TQ' denotes both Technical Quality (3.2.1) and Temporal Quality (3.2.3); Section C.5 is titled 'Content Clarity Evaluation Prompt' but contains the HERD prompt; several typos ('adpot', 'These work have proposed', 'perspectively'); some tables are dense and hard to parse (Table 3 header spans), and only three of nine models appear in the correlation analyses without clear selection rationale.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, VMBench) mostly use short, simplified prompts and low-level metrics, while long-form video generation (LVG) under complex, narrative prompts is under-evaluated.

The prompt suite construction is thoughtful: 240 prompts across 18 themes derived from real-world YouTube videos, with substantially longer (avg ~237 words) and more complex prompts (semantic/structural/control) than prior benchmarks, as quantified in Table 1.

The multi-dimensional evaluation framework is comprehensive and includes genuinely novel components: event-level alignment with Hungarian matching and order-inversion penalty (Eq. 1), transition smoothness, intra-/inter-event subject and background consistency built on an event decomposition, content clarity (TC/LS/IC/ICS), and the polarity-aware HERD protocol, which is a creative attempt to capture high-level human-expectation attributes.

Empirical coverage is broad: nine representative open-source LVG methods evaluated across 26 sub-dimensions, with useful auxiliary analyses (theme-category robustness, static-quality bias correlations, entanglement between event-level alignment and temporal consistency, prompt-complexity effects) that add credibility and diagnostic value beyond a leaderboard.

Prompts templates and implementation details are extensively documented in the appendix, and an initial prompt-suite JSON release is provided; the ethical statement addresses YouTube data collection and filtering.
weaknesses: The central claim of a 'comprehensive and reliable platform' rests almost entirely on MLLM-as-judge (Qwen2.5-VL-72B, DeepSeek-V3, Seed-1.5-VL), yet the paper provides no human validation study. There is no evidence that HERD, content clarity, or event-level alignment scores correlate with human judgments, which is the standard bar for a new benchmark's validity.

Potential circularity/bias: prompts are generated by MLLMs from reference videos, and evaluation depends on the same family of MLLMs describing and judging generated videos (including self-refine loops). Self-preference or description-generation failures could systematically distort scores, and this risk is acknowledged only obliquely (Section 4.4) rather than quantified.

Several metrics are borrowed wholesale (dynamic degree, motion smoothness, flickering from VBench; warping error and semantic consistency from EvalCrafter) with limited adaptation, and some design choices appear ad hoc (e.g., the 'Relative Reference Upper Bound' for aesthetic scores; product-of-similarities event score; variance-based transition abruptness). Sensitivity or ablation of these choices is absent.

Only multiple-choice variance mitigation for content clarity (R rounds) is reported; no confidence intervals, seed variance, or judge-model ablations (e.g., swapping Qwen2.5-VL for another VLM) are provided, so score stability across the many MLLM-dependent sub-metrics is unknown.

Reproducibility is currently incomplete: evaluation code 'will be released' after reorganization, so at submission time the benchmark cannot be fully reproduced; results depend on closed/heavy MLLMs and many tools (PySceneDetect, Grounded-SAM-2, Time-R1, DOVER++).

The headline empirical finding (models do well on static quality/short-term consistency but poorly on inter-event coherence and narrative adherence) is plausible but largely confirmatory of community expectations, and the analysis does not dig into why specific methods fail or provide actionable per-method diagnostics beyond aggregate tables.

Legal/ethical gray area: distributing prompts derived from copyrighted YouTube videos plus references to the source videos raises licensing questions; the statement asserts compliance but the released artifacts' status is not fully clarified.

Presentation issues: the five-dimension aggregation averages heterogeneous sub-metrics without justification for equal weighting; Table 2/3 percentages mix different scales; some equations (e.g., weighting constants b, c in Eq. 4) are under-specified.

strengths: Addresses a real gap: existing T2V benchmarks mostly use short, simple prompts, while LoCoT2V-Bench targets long-form (multi-scene) generation with substantially longer (avg 248 words) and more complex prompts, with a quantitative complexity comparison against prior benchmarks (Table 1, Fig. 5).

The benchmark is grounded in real-world collected videos (234 videos, 18 themes) with hierarchical metadata (characters, backgrounds, camera motions), enabling scene-aware and structured fine-grained evaluation rather than purely holistic scoring.

LoCoT2V-Eval is a thoughtfully designed multi-dimensional framework: multi-scale DeQA-based perceptual quality, coarse-to-fine text-video alignment with a hierarchical multi-turn VQA scheme that explicitly penalizes missing/hallucinated scenes, adapted streaming versions of temporal metrics for long videos, and a novel HERD metric with a dual-agent Auditor-Evaluator design intended to reduce subjectivity bias.

The paper goes beyond a single aggregate score: extensive baselines (13 LVG methods split into multi-prompt vs. direct input), category-level analyses, sub-dimension results, inter-dimension correlation analysis, and diagnostics that yield actionable findings (fine-grained alignment and character consistency are far weaker than background consistency/perceptual quality).

Human-alignment validation is non-trivial: PLCC/SRCC/KRCC across most dimensions and sub-dimensions, plus two ablations supporting design choices (character-masked vs. full-frame BC; dual-agent vs. QA-based vs. direct-scoring HERD).

Reproducibility support is strong: detailed implementation settings for all 13 baselines, full prompt templates for complexity scoring, prompt construction, and all evaluation agents in the appendix; an impact statement addresses YouTube data provenance, filtering, and content safety.
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on MLLM/LLM judges (GPT-5 for expectations/alignment scoring, an unspecified strong MLLM for verification) without systematic analysis of judge robustness, position/verbosity bias, or sensitivity to the specific model version; results may not transfer as MLLMs evolve, and the identity/version of the core judging MLLM is not clearly specified in the main text.

The human study is modest: 5% of generated videos and only three annotators, with MOS averaging; no inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Krippendorff's alpha) are reported, and no confidence intervals or significance tests accompany the method rankings in Table 2, so several close rankings may not be statistically meaningful.

The prompt 'complexity' metric is itself LLM-scored (DeepSeek-V3.2), making the headline claim of 'longer and more complex' prompts partly circular; moreover, the complexity metrics correlate only weakly (around -0.0 to -0.18) with all performance dimensions (Fig. 11), raising questions about whether the proposed complexity operationalization actually measures difficulty that matters for generation.

Several sub-dimensions show weak human alignment (e.g., Background Consistency PLCC 52.8, WE notably low, some HERD sub-dimensions around 43-49), yet these are still used as standalone leaderboard columns; the paper does not adequately discuss which sub-scores are reliable enough to support per-dimension conclusions.

HERD expectations are generated by GPT-5 from the prompt, so the 'human expectation' reference is itself model-generated; the dual-agent design mitigates but does not eliminate hallucination and the evaluation inherits LLM priors about narrative/style, which is acknowledged only obliquely (e.g., the Visual Style discrepancy).

Scale is limited: 234 prompts with a skewed length distribution and a self-acknowledged imbalance across categories; no code/data release statement is given, and reliance on closed-source APIs (GPT-5) plus proprietary baselines (Sora, Veo, Kling as motivation but not evaluated) complicates exact reproduction.

The use of YouTube-sourced videos as the basis for prompts is handled with a compliance statement, but redistribution/licensing status of the collected videos and derived prompts is not fully clarified for public release.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: evaluation of long-form video generation under complex, multi-scene prompts, where existing benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, etc.) focus on short clips and simple prompts.

The evaluation effort is substantial: 13 representative long-video generation methods are benchmarked across five major dimensions with sub-metrics, and the benchmark itself has a non-trivial construction pipeline (video collection, multi-stage MLLM prompt generation, human verification) that is documented in detail in the appendix, including full prompt templates.

The proposed HERD metric and the hierarchical multi-turn VQA alignment framework are reasonably motivated, and the paper includes useful ablations: comparison of dual-agent vs. QA-based vs. direct-scoring HERD implementations, and a character-removal ablation supporting the BC design.

A human alignment study with three annotators is provided, reporting PLCC/SRCC/KRCC across nearly all dimensions, and the identified qualitative findings (weak fine-grained alignment and character consistency despite strong background stability) are plausible and diagnostically useful.
weaknesses: Heavy and pervasive dependence on proprietary models (GPT-5, Seed1.5-VL, DeepSeek-V3.2, specific MLLMs) for both benchmark construction and evaluation. This creates serious reproducibility concerns: scores will drift as closed models change, API access and cost are barriers, and no analysis of evaluation variance (e.g., repeated runs, sensitivity to the evaluator model) is provided.

Conceptual circularity in the benchmark construction: prompts are generated by MLLMs from real videos, and evaluation is also performed by MLLMs. Models that happen to align with the distributional biases of the prompt-generating LLM may be systematically favored; this risk is not analyzed.

HERD is named 'Human Expectations Realization Degree' but the expectations are inferred by GPT-5 from the prompt, not by humans. The paper does not validate that LLM-inferred expectations match actual human expectations for a video, which is the central premise of the metric.

The human alignment study is thin: only 5% of generated videos, three annotators, no inter-annotator agreement reported, no confidence intervals or significance tests on correlations, and the proposed method only modestly outperforms the simpler QA-based baseline on several sub-dimensions (e.g., Visual Style, where it actually loses). Correlations for HERD (SRCC 58.44) and character/background consistency (49.9/51.1) are only moderate.

Scale is limited: 234 videos across 18 themes is small for a benchmark intended as a community standard, and the complexity advantage over prior benchmarks is partly self-assessed using another LLM as the judge.

Ethics/copyright treatment is asserted rather than demonstrated: videos are collected from YouTube via yt-dlp, and claiming compliance with 'the platform's terms of service and copyright regulations' is questionable, since YouTube's ToS generally prohibits downloading without permission. No discussion of licensing, takedown procedures, or whether prompts derived from copyrighted footage raise derivative-work concerns.

Several reported results are presented without statistical treatment or sanity checks (e.g., the large OA gap between LongLive at 55.50 and LongSANA at 38.06), and the relative rankings rely on a single evaluation pass with a proprietary judge.

Originality is moderate: many components are direct adaptations of existing metrics (Dynamic Degree and Motion Smoothness from VBench, wapring error from EvalCrafter, DEVIL-based DQ, CLIP-paradigm consistency), and several concurrent benchmarks already target long or complex video generation; the incremental novelty lies mainly in HERD and the fine-grained hierarchical QA scheme.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, etc.) focus on short, simple prompts, while long-form, multi-scene generation is an active area with no rigorous evaluation standard. Table 1 convincingly shows LoCoT2V-Bench's prompts are longer (248 words avg.) and more complex than all prior benchmarks.

The benchmark construction pipeline is unusually careful: MLLM-generated raw prompts are expanded, manually refined against four explicit criteria (rationality, certainty, character completeness, consistency), deduplicated for character names, safety-checked, and human-verified — with the full prompt templates reproduced in Appendix D, which aids reproducibility.

LoCoT2V-Eval is multi-dimensional and decomposed sensibly (PQ, OA/FGA, CC/BC/WE, multi-scale DQ, HERD), and the hierarchical multi-turn VQA design for fine-grained alignment, with scene-existence gating that penalizes hallucinated scenes, is a thoughtful mechanism beyond CLIP-score-style evaluation.

The evaluation effort is substantial: 13 representative LVG methods across multi-prompt and direct-input settings, category-level breakdowns, sub-dimension results, and streaming adaptations of prior metrics for long videos, making the diagnostic findings (high BC but CC < 40%, large OA→FGA drop) actionable for the community.

The human alignment study is more thorough than typical benchmark papers: three annotators, three correlation coefficients (PLCC/SRCC/KRCC), ablations of the BC computation (character removal) and of HERD implementations (QA-based and direct scoring baselines), with plausible explanations for where the proposed method underperforms (Visual Style).
Ethics treatment is appropriate: an impact statement discusses YouTube sourcing, safety filtering, PII, and the annotation procedure is described with an interface example.
weaknesses: Heavy and pervasive dependence on specific proprietary models (GPT-5 for expansion/HERD judging, Seed1.5-VL for raw prompts, DeepSeek-V3.2 for complexity scoring, plus SAM3/FG-CLIP2) creates both a reproducibility risk (closed, versioned APIs) and a potential circularity/bias concern: the same class of LLM that generates the prompts also defines the metadata, the questions, and the judgments, so scores may partly reflect MLLM priors rather than video quality. The paper does not quantify evaluator variance or test robustness to a different judge MLLM.

Scale is modest for a flagship benchmark: 234 videos/prompts, and the human alignment study covers only a 5% sample with 3 annotators. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported on the correlation results, so claims like 'HERD achieves favorable correlation' (PLCC 54.86, SRCC 58.44) rest on a small, uncharacterized sample; the Character Consistency correlation (PLCC 47.17) is only moderate.

The prompt 'complexity' scoring is validated only by a single LLM judge and, as the authors themselves concede (Fig. 11, Table 7), the complexity metrics show near-zero correlations with model performance and tiny variance — this undercuts the central narrative that prompt complexity is a meaningful benchmark axis and weakens the added value of the complexity claims.

Some design choices lack justification or error analysis: the exponential normalization for warping error, the pre-fitted linear aggregation for DQ (fit on 100 videos from the same annotators), the equal weighting of HERD dimensions, and the binary camera-movement query (a single Yes/No for prescribed cinematic motion) are all heuristic; sensitivity of results to these choices is not examined.

The HRD metric conflates the model's ability with the prompt's evaluability — LLM-inferred 'expectations' may be trivially satisfiable or ungrounded for some prompts, and the paper provides no analysis of expectation quality (e.g., inter-prompt difficulty or human agreement on the expectations themselves).

Fidelity of the YouTube-derived prompts to the source videos is asserted via human verification but not quantified; the claim of yt-dlp use 'in compliance with the platform's terms of service' is not substantiated, and no statement is made about public release of the benchmark/code, which limits reproducibility and community impact.
